name: Golden Yellow
lede: Golden yellow is a descriptive name for a warm, bright yellow, and across the centuries it has been attached to pigments, dyes and chemicals that share little beyond the adjective.

sections.title: A name that describes
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines golden yellow as a deep orangey-yellow [1]. The idea is much older than the phrase. Latin had *flavus* for the golden yellow of everything that ripens in the sun, in a vocabulary that also separated *croceus*, the saffron yellow that leans orange, from *luteus*, the dull yellow of weld and broom [4][2]. Greek used *chrysos* for golden yellow, beside separate words for ocher, greenish yellow, honey and saffron [5].

The same idea sits in scientific vocabulary. The prefix *chryso-* means golden or golden yellow, and the old word *aureate* means gold in color [1][3]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary of color (1930) lists *golden yellow* on plate 10, L 7, and our library records 1597 as the date of the name's first English use [19].

sections.title: Golden yellow in the old color schemes
sections.body:
A text in the Aristotelian corpus, *On Colours*, names only white and golden yellow as primaries and ties them to the elements [8]. Gage notes that the ninth-century Syrian writer Job of Edessa, whose *Book of Treasures* leaned on Greek theory, treated black and white as primary and counted golden-yellow among the intermediate colors [10]. In his Cambridge lectures of 1669 and 1670, Newton set out a scale of the prism that listed lemon yellow and golden yellow, or sun-gold, as separate steps [11].

None of these writers meant a single paint. The phrase marked a place on a scale, between pale lemon and a darker yellow.

sections.title: One name, many materials
sections.body:
As a pigment name it was never stable. The nineteenth-century color writers Field, in 1835, and Salter, in a later edition of 1869, used *golden yellow* alongside golden sulfur of antimony for an orange antimony pigment whose composition remains unclear [12]. The Colour Index entry for lead iodide, CI 77613, calls it a golden yellow pigment used in mosaic gold [13]. The Pigment Compendium adds that mosaic gold is normally the name of tin(IV) sulfide, a bronze or golden yellow compound that decomposes at 600 degrees Celsius [13]. Painters used mosaic gold as a false gold [6].

Better-known yellows were described the same way. Naples yellow runs from pale to golden yellow [17], and [[indian-yellow]] gives a deep golden yellow that suits watercolor better than oil [9]. Lead chromates, first made in the early nineteenth century, ranged from golden yellow through orange to red [16]. Watin advised in 1785 that the buckthorn berries for a yellow lake called stil de grain should be chosen for a golden yellow color, which gives a jonquil tint [14]. Among dyes, chrysaniline, a golden-yellow dye, is also called aniline yellow [3].

The great painters' yellow of the old workshop gets the same adjective. Rubens used lead-tin yellow for the golden-yellow touches of his portrait of himself and his wife, and that pigment was the key yellow from the fifteenth century to the middle of the eighteenth [15]. For other yellows near this one, see [[orpiment]], [[ochre]], [[lemon-yellow]] and [[mustard]].

sections.title: What it stood for
sections.body: Pastoureau writes that ripe wheat, grain, fruit, honey and the coats of some sheep and cattle gave golden yellow a favorable symbolism in Egypt, Greece and Rome: light, warmth, happiness, fertility and prosperity [4]. When Van Gogh arrived in the south of France, he wrote to his brother Theo that the sun gave a light he could only call yellow, and the words he reached for included sulfur, lemon and golden [7]. In the United States, since 1893, colleges have used a code of academic colors for their faculties; golden yellow stands for science [18].

sections.title: Three goldens on one name
sections.body: The swatch on this page, #FFDF00, comes from a Wikipedia list [19]. The nearest ISCC-NBS category is "brilliant yellow", 5.1 units away, and the nearest name in our library is [[gold]], 2.5 units away [19]. But RAL 1004, which carries the name "golden yellow" in the industrial list of 1927, is a deeper amber of about #E49E00 on screen, some 32 units from our swatch [19]. The xkcd color survey's version, #FEC615, sits between the two, 16 units from ours [19]. The name stretches from a lemon-leaning gold to an amber, and which you get depends on the list. A screen value for a RAL color is only approximate [19].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Golden yellow at this brightness is nearly absent from painting. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a painting-wide test finds it in one, and the stricter test that compares colors within each painting finds it in two [20]. That makes it rarer than 82 per cent of the colors we have names for [20]. The count says the color is rare, not why; a clean, bright yellow of this strength is far from the muted yellows of aged oil paint. Like every number here, it comes from photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [20]. The contrast with [[amber]], [[yellow]] and [[goldenrod]], which painters and dyers used in quantity, is part of the point: the name is old, the exact color is a screen color.

questions.q: Which Latin word names the golden yellow of everything that ripens in the sun?
Golden yellow has always named one specific pigment.

openers: The name golden yellow has been used for an antimony pigment, a lead compound, a buckthorn lake and a dye, with no single material behind it [12][13][14][3].
RAL's golden yellow is a deeper amber, about 32 units from the bright yellow swatch usually shown under this name [19].
